column4: The section's action-known horse reappears explicitly in the evening display of “الصَّافِنَاتُ الْجِيَادُ”; the horses here are poised and presented, extending the image from exertion to valued form.
The section stages horses rushing into a group; this verse names “رِبَاطِ الْخَيْلِ” prepared as military force, giving the mounted-charge scene its place in deliberate preparation and deterrence.
The section links the human to the animal's rider-facing side and treats the horse as cherished property; this verse explicitly gives “الْخَيْلَ” for riding and adornment, joining service to display.
The section says the horse is both a running animal and a beloved possession; this list places “الْخَيْلِ الْمُسَوَّمَةِ” among what people desire and love, making that double role explicit.

The section directly connects its “love of good/wealth” wording to this horse scene: “حُبَّ الْخَيْرِ عَنْ ذِكْرِ رَبِّي” joins horses, intense love, and remembrance of the Lord, while the section preserves both readings of عَنْ.
The section explicitly compares its action-named oath to this opening, “الصَّافَّاتِ صَفًّا”; this verse contributes the first role in the same compact oath by an active feminine plural group.
In the oath form the section identifies, “فَالزَّاجِرَاتِ زَجْرًا” adds a next, forceful action after the ranks, paralleling the linked stages of the horse charge without equating their actors.
The section explicitly cites “الْمُرْسَلَاتِ عُرْفًا” as an action-led oath; this verse establishes a group named by what it does, like the successive doers in 100:1–5.
The section explicitly cites the following “فَالْعَاصِفَاتِ عَصْفًا”; this verse supplies a forceful next movement joined by ف, matching the section's linked oath stages.
The section's horse runs ahead and its chest wins the race; “فَالسَّابِقَاتِ سَبْقًا” gives a direct race-ahead role inside another staged oath sequence.
Surah 100:9 and this verse share “بُعْثِرَ” with the graves: the horse image's human turn ends at what comes out of burial, and this verse states that overturning directly.
The section's dust-raising charge gives way to the buried world's disclosure; here “أَثْقَالَهَا” are thrown up by the earth, a concrete companion scene to the graves opened in 100:9.
The section contrasts the horse's chest that wins visibly with the human chest whose contents are brought out; this verse says God knows “مَا تُخْفِي الصُّدُورُ,” naming what the judgment discloses.
The section's inner contents are sifted after burial is undone; “يَوْمَ تُبْلَى السَّرَائِرُ” gives the parallel scene of hidden inward things being exposed.
The section says the human is witness to his own ingratitude, unlike the horse whose performance attests to its quality; “بَصِيرَةٌ عَلَىٰ نَفْسِهِ” makes the self the witness despite excuses.
For the section's human who is himself witness to his conduct, this verse says “كَفَىٰ بِنَفْسِكَ الْيَوْمَ عَلَيْكَ حَسِيبًا,” making the person his own reckoner.
The section sets the horse's bodily performance as its evidence against the human's self-witness; here “أَلْسِنَتُهُمْ وَأَيْدِيهِمْ وَأَرْجُلُهُم” bear witness to what people did.
The section makes a runner's own body attest to its performance; here mouths are sealed while “أَيْدِيهِمْ” speak and “أَرْجُلُهُم” testify against people.
The section's horse is witnessed through its bodily action, while the human is answerable for his own; here hearing, sight, and skin bear witness against the people themselves.

The section's dictionary entry uses صَدَرَ الفَرَس for a horse that finishes ahead on its chest; here “يَصْدُرُ النَّاسُ” sends people out in scattered groups to see their deeds, turning the chest/race image toward reckoning.
The section notes that “al-khayr” in 100:8 can mean wealth; here “خَيْرًا” is a good deed that its doer will see, contrasting the coveted good/property with good that is actually done.

The section's dictionary branch for جَمْعًا says a horse gathers its whole run in one surge; “جَمَعَ مَالًا وَعَدَّدَهُ” uses that root for a person accumulating and counting wealth, reversing concentrated motion into hoarding.
The section calls the human intensely attached to “good/wealth”; “وَتُحِبُّونَ الْمَالَ حُبًّا جَمًّا” states that attachment as abundant love of wealth.
The section places a horse and love of wealth beside “my Lord”; this verse marks the boundary where beloved wealth, trade, and homes are dearer than God, His Messenger, and striving in His cause.
The section says the source's dictionary form شَدّ names the horse's run while the human is “shadīd” in love of wealth; “أَشَدُّ حُبًّا لِلَّهِ” redirects that intensity of love toward God.
Against the section's human clinging to wealth, this verse makes giving from what one loves a condition of reaching righteousness: “مِمَّا تُحِبُّونَ.”
The section shows love of wealth as the human counterpart to a horse's service; this verse's righteous person gives “الْمَالَ عَلَىٰ حُبِّهِ,” turning attachment into care for others.
The section's horse is the animal under a rider; this verse says God made livestock and ships among what people ride, setting that mounted relation within provision from the Lord.
The preceding 43:12 establishes the mount; this verse's own “عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِ” turns riding into remembrance of the Lord's favor, the response set against 100:6's ingratitude.
After 43:12–13 name the mount and remembrance of its favor, this verse completes the rider's words with “إِلَىٰ رَبِّنَا لَمُنقَلِبُونَ,” returning the scene to the Lord.

The section says the animal gives its body to its owner's work; this passage begins by saying livestock were created for people and “فَهُمْ لَهَا مَالِكُونَ,” grounding that service in divine provision.
Following 36:71's livestock belonging to people, this verse says they were subdued and some are mounts; it supplies the bodily service that the section sets against human ingratitude.
After 36:71–72 name livestock, their subjection, and riding, this verse names their benefits and asks “أَفَلَا يَشْكُرُونَ”; gratitude is the explicit opposite of the human's كَنُود.
The section follows horses moving at dawn; this verse notices livestock's beauty both when brought home and when sent out, giving the animal's daily departure and return a valued human-facing scene.

The section's source gloss for الإنسان places the rider beside the animal; this verse says livestock carry people's heavy loads to places they could not reach without difficulty, making the mount's service concrete.

38:31–32 establish the displayed horses and Solomon's ambiguous words about love and remembrance; this verse itself returns the horses and names “السُّوقِ وَالْأَعْنَاقِ,” keeping the bodily horse scene present without resolving the ambiguity.
The section's horse expends its run for an owner; Satan is told to rally “بِخَيْلِكَ وَرَجِلِكَ,” a specific reversal in which mounted force serves a misleading cause.
The section reads 100:1–5 as a linked oath sequence; “وَالذَّارِيَاتِ ذَرْوًا” begins another oath by an active feminine plural group, contributing its first staged role.
In that separate oath sequence, “فَالْحَامِلَاتِ وِقْرًا” supplies a next role joined by ف, matching the section's movement from one action to another.
“فَالْجَارِيَاتِ يُسْرًا” names smooth running in the same linked oath sequence, a direct movement parallel to the section's fast-running animal.
“فَالْمُقَسِّمَاتِ أَمْرًا” completes this oath's sequence with an assigned act; like 100:1–5, the verse participates in an oath built from successive doers.
The section's cited oath continues in this verse with “وَالنَّاشِرَاتِ نَشْرًا”; its own contribution is another action-named collective in the staged sequence.
“فَالْفَارِقَاتِ فَرْقًا” adds a further act to the oath sequence the section compares with 100:1–5, joined by the same stepwise ف.
“فَالْمُلْقِيَاتِ ذِكْرًا” is the next active role in the sequence; it extends the action-led oath form that the section uses to read the horse's successive movements.
The identity of this oath's actors is debated; on its wording, “وَالنَّازِعَاتِ غَرْقًا” opens another sequence of feminine plural action-titles, matching the section's action-named oath group.
This verse adds “وَالنَّاشِطَاتِ نَشْطًا” to that active feminine-plural oath sequence, paralleling the section's way of identifying a collective by its movement.
“وَالسَّابِحَاتِ سَبْحًا” names a moving group within the oath sequence, a motion-stage parallel to the section's linked run and charge.
“فَالْمُدَبِّرَاتِ أَمْرًا” completes the sequence of active oath-titles; the section's point is likewise that successive roles, not an animal's name, carry the opening image.

This verse immediately precedes the horse display in 38:31 and calls Solomon “نِعْمَ الْعَبْدُ” who repeatedly turned back to God; it frames, without deciding, the following horse-and-remembrance statement.

The section treats horses as both valued possessions and working bodies; this verse calls wealth and children adornment of worldly life and contrasts them with enduring righteous deeds, clarifying what the horse's visible value cannot secure.
The section notes that “al-khayr” can mean wealth in its line about love; here “خَيْرًا” is what someone leaves as an estate, a concrete Qur'anic use of that dictionary sense.

The section's dictionary branch for جَمْعًا describes a horse gathering its run in one charge; “جَمَعَ فَأَوْعَىٰ” instead describes a person collecting and hoarding, turning gathered force into possession.
The section sets the horse's charge beside human attachment to wealth; “أَلْهَاكُمُ التَّكَاثُرُ” names abundance-rivalry as a human preoccupation, a specific social counterpart to that attachment.
After 102:1 names rivalry in abundance, this verse says it lasts “حَتَّىٰ زُرْتُمُ الْمَقَابِرَ”; it brings the property race to the grave scene that follows the horse image in Surah 100.
The section's animal races into a crowd while the human clings to wealth; “سَابِقُوا إِلَىٰ مَغْفِرَةٍ” redirects racing toward forgiveness from the Lord.
After 3:14 lists the loved horses and other desires, this verse says “وَسَارِعُوا إِلَىٰ مَغْفِرَةٍ,” offering a specific opposite direction for human urgency.
Following 3:133's call to hasten toward forgiveness, this verse describes those who spend in ease and hardship; it gives a concrete alternative to the section's human attachment to wealth.
After 99:7 says a deed of good will be seen, this verse completes the pair with a deed of evil; it extends the section's own-witness motif to both sides of the human account.
82:4 has just overturned the graves, paralleling 100:9; this verse adds that every soul will know what it sent ahead and left behind, completing the disclosure of deeds.
The section ends its human contrast with what is brought out from within; “وَإِذَا الصُّحُفُ نُشِرَتْ” gives a neighboring judgment scene in which the records themselves are opened.
The section's image turns from the horse's winning chest to what is sifted from human chests; this verse says God tests “مَا فِي صُدُورِكُمْ” and purifies what is in hearts.
The section asks the reader to picture what is brought out of the chest; this verse asks whether God will not bring out “أَضْغَانَهُمْ,” naming concealed resentment as inward content.

The section ends with the Lord fully aware of people on the day their inward contents are exposed; this verse expressly joins what people conceal and reveal with God's knowledge of “ذَاتِ الصُّدُورِ.”
41:20 has just named hearing, sight, and skin as witnesses; this verse's own question to their skins makes bodily testimony answerable, paralleling the section's body-as-evidence image.

After 41:20–21 make the body testify, this verse says people did not hide from those witnesses but thought God did not know much of their deeds, a direct boundary against the Lord's knowledge in 100:11.

The section distinguishes the horse's own performance as witness from the human's ingratitude; this verse says the human has only what he strives for, keeping effort and its account attached to the doer.

The section makes the horse's hard breathing audible in its run; this verse describes the human as “كَادِحٌ” laboring toward the Lord until meeting Him, shifting exertion from the charge to an inevitable encounter.

The section's dictionary form describes a racehorse made lean like an arrow-shaft; this verse also pictures a lean mount, a camel coming from distant passes for pilgrimage, though its leanness reflects travel rather than the horse's training.
